# Introduction

The eastern oyster (*Crassostrea virginica*) is a foundational species that provides numerous ecosystem goods and services such as food and habitat production, shoreline stabilization and protection, water quality improvement, nutrient cycling, and carbon sequestration [@Geselbracht2024; @Grabowski2012; @Barnes2007]. Additionally, eastern oystershave been estimnated to generate up to nearly $100,000/ha in economic value as the species suppoirts numerous industries and activities such as commerical fisheries, eco-tourism, and recreational harvesting [@Geselbracht2024; @LaPeyre2021; @Grabowski2012].

In recent decades, oyster reefs have experienced substantial declines, with only an estimated 15% remaining worldwide, including an estimated 50-80% decline in habitat within the Gulf of Mexico region alone [@Pollack2012; @LaPeyre2021]. The decline is largely attributed to a range of anthropogenic related activities such as overharvesting, habitat alteration, sedimentation and water quality decline, disease, and changing hydrology [@LaPeyre2021; @Geselbracht2024]. In response to these sharp declines, many restoration efforts have been undertaken with varying strategies and success rates; recently, planning documents released by the Deepwater Horizon Natural Resource Damage Assessment Trustees called for large-scale development of reef networks to increase resilience [@Geselbracht2024].

## Oyster decline in the Pensacola Bay System

One such system to experience oyster decline is the Pensacola Bay System (PBS). The PBS is a large estuarine system located in Escambia and Santa Rosa counties in northwest Florida. The system is comprised of multiple water bodies including Pensacola Bay, Escambia Bay, Blackwater Bay, East Bay, and Santa Rosa Sound; and is influenced heavily by freshwater input from the Escambia, Blackwater and Yellow Rivers [@Christensen1997]. Historically, the PBS supported extensive oyster reefs that provided critical habitat for a variety of species and substantial economic value to the surrounding communities [@Christensen1997]. However, over the past several decades, the extent of oyster habitat within the PBS has declined significantly due to a combination of factors including overharvesting, habitat degradation, and water quality issues. One estimate puts the decline in oyster habitat from 15,000 ha in 1883 to 91.5 ha in 2021 [@Geselbracht2024]. This decline has prompted efforts to restore oyster reefs within the PBS [@PPBEP_OysterRestoration; @TNC2021OysterRestoration], with multiple studies aiming to identify the most suitable areas within the estuary to focus restoration efforts [@Geselbracht2024; @Christensen1997; @PPBEP_OysterRestoration].

With limited resources available for restoration, it is critical to identify areas where chances of oyster survival and long-term reef establishment are at their highest, as poor site selection could ultimately lead to unsatisfactory results. As with any ecosystem, the environmental conditions within the PBS vary greatly in time and space, and such variations can have great impacts on oyster survival and establishment. Therefore, it is important to understand the environmental factors that drive oyster occurrence, so that scientists and policymakers can make informed decisions regarding said restoration site selection [@Pollack2012; @Barnes2007; @Geselbracht2024].

## Environmental controls on Eastern oyster habitat

Oyster recruitment, survival, and reef establishment are influenced by complex interactions between numerous physical, chemical, and biological environmental factors. As such, determining the most influential factors is a multivariate problem that requires careful consideration of each factor and its interactions with others [@LaPeyre2021; @Pollack2012; @Barnes2007; @Christensen1997]. To help narrow the focus, the most commonly cited environmental factors were examined in the literature and are summarized here. 
   
Perhaps the most influential and widely reported environmental driver of oyster suitability is salinity, which represents an important environmental gradient within estuarine systems that influences physiology, recruitment, disease, predation, and survival. Other important characteristics often reported are shown in @tbl-environmental-drivers and include dissolved oxygen, temperature, depth, turbidity, and bottom type (substrate) [@LaPeyre2021; @Pollack2012; @Barnes2007; @Geselbracht2024; @Christensen1997].

It should be recognized that not all environmental factors are often not adequately spatially distributed or represented within the available datasets, and therefore careful consideration should be given when selecting the final dataset used for modeling habitat suitability [@LaPeyre2021; @Geselbracht2024; @Christensen1997].

## Species Distribution Modelling

Quantifying the relationships between the distribution of species and the species-environment interactions has a long history in ecological research, having been described as far back as the late 17th and early 18th centuries in which researchers observed biological patterns in terms of their relationships with geographical and/or environmental gradients [@Rushton2004; @Elith2009]. Since then, the propagation of large-scale spatial datasets, the development and integration of GIS, increased access to statistical packages and computational power has opened up the oppurtunity for researchers to explore increased model complexity utilizing multipe interactions between species and their environment [@Johnson2005]. Species Distribution Modeling (SDM) is one area that has benefited largely over recent years. SDMs are loosely defined as numerical tools that combine observations of species occurrence or abundance with environmental estimates [@Elith2009]. Further, @Elith2009 described SDMs as being able to be integrated into several different families of models. These  classifications include: expert-driven or heuristic, environmental-envelope, environmental-similarity, regression-based, Bayesian and hierarchical, machine-learning and data mining, and ensemble or multimodal [@Elith2009]. As such, deciding on which type of SDM largely depends on a multitude of factors such as the study's objective, quality and quantity of available data, ecological characteristics of the species, spatial and temporal scale, whether input data includes absence data or presence-only data [@Elith2009].

*Habitat Suitability Indices*

One popular approach used in many studies involving the Eastern oyster throughout the gulf region are Habitat Suitability Indeces (HSIs) [@Barnes2007; @Pollack2012; @Geselbracht2024; @Christensen1997]. HSIs are typically used in situations where quantitative data on species distributions is difficult to collect or non-existent, relying on expert-driven variable selection, meta-analysis, and classification methods that transform environmental characteristics into standardized estimates of habitat suitability [@Barnes2007; @Pollack2012; @Geselbracht2024; @Johnson2005]. 

Within the PBS, HSIs have been used to develop GIS-based habitat suitability models (HSMs) that integrate biological, physical, chemical, and management-related variables in order to identify suitable restoration areas with the system. In the mid 1990's @Christensen1997 developed an HSI for the eastern oyster in the PBS to demonstrate the model framework's usefulness in illustrating species suitability in a system wide approach. @Geselbracht2024 then followed and further expanded on the approach incorporating management factors into the model, adding a layer of regulatory influence to the model output versus the purely environmental analysis of the prior. Additionally, the Pensacola and Perdido Bay Estuary Program recently built on-top of @Geselbracht2024 by incorporating some of their own data and refining some of the weighting [@PPBEP_OysterRestoration].

These previous studies alone highlight the strengths and weaknesses of the HSI approaches. Some of the strengths include interoperability, adaptability, and the integration of ecological knowledge, but the results entirely rely on expert decisions regarding variable selection, suitability functions, weighting and scoring, and how to aggregate the results. All of these present opportunity for differing outputs even if the same inputs were used by different groups [@Geselbracht2024; @Johnson2005]. Furthere, these models are often estuary specific, meaning that practitioners must start from the beginning with each new ecological system. 

*Maximum Entropy Modelling (MaxEnt)*

MaxEnt is a presence-background SDM framework based on general-purpose machine learning methods that are useful for making predictions using incomplete information by relating environmental conditions at known occurrence locations to the environmental conditions throughout the study area [@Phillips2006; @Elith2011]. Some of the main benefits of MaxEnt is that it uses presence-only data, reducing the need for the often unavailable absence data, it has the ability to model complex interactions between environmental conditions, and it has demonstrated high predictive performance while limiting overfitting through regularization [@Phillips2009; @Merow2013; @Elith2011]. The fact that MaxEnt modeling is tailored to presence only modeling is especially useful here as there is an existing dataset featuring oyster presence locations in which the Florida Wildlife Commission explicitly collected occurrence data without including absence locations [@FWC2026].

However, the use of such algorithms should not be made blindly as many issues can arise if careful precautions are not taken. Due to the complexity and inter-connectivity of ecosystems, many biases in the data samples can arise such as spatial and temporal autocorrelation, group dependence structures, hierarchical structures and multicollinearity leading to overfitting model parameters and over-optimistic prediction confidence [@Dormann2013; @Kass2021; @Roberts2017]. Thankfully, significant work has been put into this through cross-validation techniques and the development of model evaluation software packages such as ENMeval 2.0 implemented through the R statistical language [@Kass2021; @Roberts2017] 

## Study Objective

To demonstrate how a MaxEnt SDM can be used as a complementary tool to help researchers and practitioners leading ecological restoration activities, this study aims to develop an empirically fitted MaxEnt habitat-suitability model using observed oyster occurrence data and known environmental conditions. The primary objective will be to develop a spatially explicit SDM representing relative Eastern oyster habitat suitability throughout the PBS. Next, the resulting suitability surface will be evaluated against the existing Pensacola Bay HSI developed by @Geselbracht2024 and iterated upon by @PPBEP_OysterRestoration. To achieve this, environmental predictors that are commonly associated with oyster habitat suitability will be identified and obtained. The predictors will be used to fit the MaxEnt model and model performance will be evaluated using spatially separated cross-validation. Finally, we will compare the predicted surface to the existing HSI to determine areas of agreement and disagreement, and we will use these results to determine whether the MaxEnt framework provides an empirical alternative or complement to HSI-based restoration planning. It is hypothesized that the MaxEnt model will successfully identify patterns of habitat suitability for the eastern oyster within the PBS. Overall agreement between the HSI and MaxEnt is expected to be high. However, MaxEnt is expected to produce a smoother, more continuous suitability surface because of the empirically fitted environmental relationships as opposed to predefined, lower-resolution HSI suitability envelopes. As a result, the MaxEnt model could prove beneficial to help narrow down project locations to help reinforce expert-driven model outputs.

All data analysis and processing was performed using the R programming language [@r]. Environmental observation data was acquired from the EPA's Water Quality Portal via the dataRetrieval r-package [@wqp_2026; @dataRetrieval2026]. To avoid distortion, all spatial data was projected to the NAD83(2011) / Florida North State Plane Coordinate System (EPSG:6440) with distances in meters. A full list of r packages will be provied in the supplemental section.

As previously described, the study area for this project is the Pensacola Bay System which includes portions of Pensacola Bay, Escambia Bay, East Bay and Blackwater Bay [@fig-study-area]. Boundaries of this study area were determined by using the Florida Department of Environmental Protections (FDEP) Waterbody IDs ArcGIS Online feature [@FDEP2005WBIDs]. The dataset was filtered to include only relevant WBIDs (nine IDs in the 548 series) and then combined to create a singular study area polygon. This polygon also served as a spatial filter and was used to extract relevant environmental data from much larger datasets in the coming data gathering. The chosen WBIDs were used in order to match the previous study area applied in @Geselbracht2024 and @PPBEP_OysterRestoration.

Oyster occurrence data was acquired from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Commission's GIS portal as polygons and converted to points using polygon centroids [@FWC2026]. Salinity, dissolved oxygen, temperature, turbidity, and chlorophyll-a observations were obtained from the Water Quality Portal using the 'dataRetrieval' package in R for all sites located within the PBS and collected within the 20 year period from 2005 to 2025 [@wqp_2026; @dataRetrieval2026]. Parameters were chosen based on relevance and representation in previous oyster habitat restoration studies [@LaPeyre2021; @Barnes2007; @Pollack2012; @Geselbracht2024]. Bathymetry data for the PBS was obtained from NOAA [@NOAA_2018]. Bottom sediment data and oyster recruitment data was obtained from the Pensacola and Perdido Bay Estuary Program although the data source attribution originally belongs to @Macauley2005 and @Arnold2017, respectively.

All water quality parameters were inspected to ensure comparable measurement units and analytical procedures to avoid combining different forms of similar analytes. To avoid extereme outliers leading to sskewed data, all raw datasets first underwent an outlier detection screening using the inter-quartile range (IQR) to flag potential outliers. Outliers were defined as follows:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Outlier if } \quad
x &< Q_{0.25} - 1.5(IQR) \\
\text{or} \quad
x &> Q_{0.75} + 1.5(IQR) \\
\
\text{where } IQR &= Q_{0.75} - Q_{0.25}
\end{aligned}
$$

The data was then filtered to include only observations collected during the warm season (May through October). To reduce spatial bias, where certain locations were monitored much more heavily and much more often then others, all stations were averaged to one value per unique station per year. Finally, the annual means were averaged so that only one overall representative value for each unique location ID. However, significant spatial clustering remained, so station means were averaged within 2 km hexagonal bins, and converted to a centroid to represent the overall conditions for that 2km region.

## Environmental Prediction Rasters

Prior to use in the MaxEnt modeling framework, continuous prediction rasters were created for dissolved oxygen, salinity, turbidity, and water temperature using the Inverse Path Distance Weighting (IPDW) package in R [@IPDW_2023]. IPDW is a variant of Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW), which is a deterministic interpolation method that allows for the estimation of point values using the equation:

$$ 
V= \frac{\sum\limits^{n}_{i=1} v_i {d^{-p}_{i}}}{\sum\limits^{n}_{i=1} {d^{-p}_{i}}} 
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the prediction and measurement points, $v_i$ is the parameter value, and $p$ is a power parameter. However, in IPDW $d$ is a calculated path-distance value rather than a typical Euclidean distance as used in IDW [@Stachelek2015].

IPDW was selected due to the model's ability to be barrier aware and avoid interference or influence from crossing land boundaries that can be introduced when using more traditional Euclidean based interpolation methods [@Stachelek2015]. This is especially important given the geography of the study area where the Garcon Point area is a narrow, low lying peninsula separating Escambia Bay to the west and Blackwater Bay to the east. Both of which are significantly influenced by different riverine inputs. Instead, IPDW weighs observations according to the shortest water-path distance through the aquatic environment.

Model sensitivity was evaluated for distance power and max interpolation range for each parameter. In IPDW, distance power determines how rapidly a site's influence decays as path distance increases. The tested powers ($p$) were 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00, 1.25, 1.50, 2.00, 2.50, and 3.00. The tested ranges were 5, 10, 15, and 20 km. All combinations were evaluated for each parameter.

Spatial cross-validation was used to determine interpolation accuracy using the blockCV package in R, which uses spatial folds to split data into test and training data sets [@Valavi2019]. To assess sensitivity to the spatial split, the fold-generation procedure was repeated, each time refitting the IPDW model and comparing the results to the held-out observation spatial-blocks. For this analysis 5 spatial folds were used with 5 km spatial blocks, and blocks were assigned to folds randomly. This process was then repeated across 5 random seeds in which a new spatial partition was generated for each seed. For each spatial fold, the monitoring locations were used in the training data to construct the IPDW prediction surface. Withheld monitoring locations were used to extract predicted values from the prediction raster and compared to the observed station means.

Finally, model performance was evaluated using calculated prediction-error statistics for each distance power - max range combination. Each statistic was summarized across each repetition to generate a mean absolute error (MAE), the standard deviation of the MAE, the mean root mean squared error (RMSE) and its standard deviation, the mean prediction bias (+/-) and finally the prediction coverage. Mean MAE was the primary metric used in parameter selection, although in cases where differences between several of the lowest results were negligible, the smoother surfaces were given preference to better reflect the reality of a well mixed natural system.

The final prediction surfaces were generated by fitting the IPDW algorithm using the selected distance power and range on the full dataset for each environmental variable. The selected settings were evaluated using 5 km spatial blocks and five folds to calculate MAE, RMSE, prediction bias, and prediction coverage.

## Oyster Occurence and Background Data

Oyster occurrence data had to go through some processing prior to being used in the MaxEnt model. To avoid introducing unwanted spatial bias in the model, the original 443 processed occurence locations were spatially thinned to 1 km per point using the GeoThinneR package [@GeoThinneR]. MaxEnt also requires the use of background data, which are points who's locations characterize available environmental conditions without being treated as oyster absences [@Phillips2006; @Elith2011; @Phillips2009]. Randomly generated background points (n = 10,000) were randomly generated in areas that had complete prediction raster coverage, excluding any cells that already contained a presence location. 

## MaxEnt Species Distribution Modeling

The species distribution model was fit, tuned and evaluated using the ENMeval package in R (@Kass2021). A presence-background MaxEnt framework was used via the "maxnet" algorithm included in said package. The final environmental predictors used were dissolved oxygen, salinity, sediment, turbidity, water temperature, and oyster recruitment. Sediment was treated as a factor with codes 1, 2, and 3, representing mud, muddy sand, and sand, respectively. The prediction domain was reduced to include areas that had a prediction cell value for each of the prediction variables. 

Spatial cross-validation was performed using ENMeval's included four-partition block method. This method divides occurrences geographically by northing, then easting, and finally assigns background points to each of the blocks. Four model candidates were evaluated for performance with increasing complexity using different combinations of regularization techniques: linear (L), linear and quadratic (LQ), linear, quadratic and hinge (LQH), and linear, quadratic, hinge and interaction (LQHP). Each of these combinations were tested with six regularization multipliers (0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, and 4), resulting in 24 total model candidates with 96 fold evaluations. 

The cross-validation results were used in selecting the optimal model settings, via a sequential method that selected models with the lowest average 10 percentile omission rate, and if needed as a tie breaker, the settings that resulted in the highest average validation Continuous Boyce Index [@Hirzel2006]. Finally, the selected model was fit to all oyster occurrence and background data points to generate the final suitability raster.

## HSI vs MaxEnt Comparison

A modified habitat suitability index (HSI) was created using similar methods presented in @Geselbracht2024. The data and methods used were based on a PPBEP adaption of the original HSI. Original input data was able to be obtained from PPBEP unfortunately the exact HSI model was no longer available so it had to be recreated using their provided methodology. The HSI was created using ArcGis Pro Suitability Modeler, with the input rasters transformed into suitability scores and subsequently combined using percentage weights. Environmental data used included salinity, temperature, dissolved oxygen, chlorophyll-a, and turbidity, with only observations collected between May through October in the years 2017 - 2023. It should be noted that this data was provided as-is and as such, should not be considered equal to the previously created environmental rasters in this study. The HSI also included the same sediment and larval dispersal data used here. Finally, the model included 2021 oyster distribution data, though it is not confirmed whether it is the same dataset obatained earlier in this study. Each variable was rated from 1 through 10, with all variables recieving a 1, 5 or 10. Where 1 = low, 5 = moderate, and 10 = high. @tbl-hsi-classification-table describes each classification or transformation that was used. The HSI model output was then normalized via Min-Max Normalization using the ArcGIS Pro Raster Calculator.

To ensure raster alignment, both the HSI and MaxEnt surfaces were projected to the Florida State Plane North coordinate reference system, and resampled to 100m using bilinear resampling. A coverage mask was created to ensure only cells that had values within both rasters were used in the comparison. Finally, the rasters were classified using equal intervals using breaks 0, 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80 and 1. The resulting classes were labeled low, intermediate-low, intermediate, intermediate-high, and high, respectively.  

Classified prediction raster agreement was described by determining the count of cells of exact agreement, the count of cells in close-agreement (i.e. those that fell within one class), and finally by utilizing continuous Spearman correlation. Additionally, spatial agreement was evaluated mathematically by subtracting the values of the HSI from the values of the MaxEnt prediction surfaces. This would result in a divergent comparison matrix in which negative values would indicate areas that the MaxEnt model favored, values at or close to zero represent areas where the models agreed, and postive values showed areas that the HSI favored.

Processing resulted in 27 binned values using 666. Dissolved Oxygen had 6,261 observations from 169 sites. Processing reduced the data to 68 binned values using 3,010 observations. Each parameter (save for chlorophyll-a) was interpolated into predicted surface rasters using an inverse-path distance weighting algorithm. To ensure the highest accuracy was achieved, a sensitivy analysis was conducted on each parameter model using 36 distance-power/range combinations, which were in turn evaluated across five random five-fold spatial partitions. Powers ranged from 0.25 to 3.00, and  maximum range values evaluated were 5, 10, 15, and 20 km (@fig-ipdw-sensitivity). 

While the results of every sensitivity analysis will be reported here, it should be noted that after running all parameters it was decided that a distance power of 0.25 and a max range of 10km was to be used. This decision was made as there was little variation in results of the sensitivity analysis and a smoother prediction surface was preferred to better represent the smoother gradients found in the real world.

::: {.cell-output-display}

### Dissolved Oxygen

Dissolved oxygen sensitivity had a mean MAE ranging from 0.426 to 0.507 mg/L. The lowest mean MAE with 100% prediction was 0.425mg/L using a distance power of 0.75 and max range of 10km (@tbl-ipdw-validation). The predicted rater surface values ranged from 5.28mg/L to 7.99mg/L (n = 33,792; µ = 6.52; σ = 0.26; @tbl-raster-summary). The final prediction model achieved 100% coverage with a MAE of 0.431 mg/L (σ = 0.006) with RMSE = 0.552 mg/L (σ = 0.004). The model tended to over predict by +0.013 mg/L. Spatially, dissolved oxygen generally decreased in the western portions of the study area. With the lowest values appearing in East Bay and northern Blackwater Bay (@fig-environmental-rasters).   


### Salinity

The salinity sensitivity analysis had a mean MAE ranging from 2.397 ppt to 3.125 ppt. The lowest reported MAE with 100% model coverage was 2.49 ppt using distance power 0.50 and max range of 10km. The absolute lowest mean MAE was 2.397 ppt was achieved using distance power of 3.00 and a max range of 5km , but model coverage fell to 96.1%. The difference in mean MAE between the lowest achieved DP-MR combination and the actual DP-MR combination used was 0.000119 ppt (@tbl-ipdw-validation). Spatial cross-validation of the final model fit had a MAE of 2.49 ppt (σ = 0.036) and RMSE 3.444 ppt (σ = 0.024). The model slightly over predicted salinity values (+0.140 ppt) and achieved 100% coverage. The predicted values ranged from 2.31 to 26.73 ppt (n = 33,792; µ = 16.36 ppt; σ = 3.14; @tbl-raster-summary). Spatially, salinity generally decreased from west to east with the lowest values being in the northern Blackwater Bay and the highest values located in the southwestern region of Pensacola Bay (@fig-environmental-rasters).

## MaxEnt Model Tuning and Selection

Overall, the models performed moderately at best with 16 of the 24 candidate models having $\bar{AUC} \le 0.50$. Across the 24 candidate models, training AUC ranged from 0.747 to 0.863, while mean validation AUC ranged from 0.460 to 0.703. Mean validation Continuous Boyce Index (CBI) ranged from −0.353 to 0.334, and mean 10th-percentile omission rates ranged from 0.115 to 0.250. AICc values ranged from 677.70 to 693.66, with model complexity ranging from 3 to 14 nonzero coefficients.

Selected Model Performance

The selected model used linear, quadratic, and hinge (LQH) features with a regularization multiplier of 0.5 [@tbl-maxent-selection]. This configuration achieved the highest mean validation AUC (0.703 ± 0.136 SD) and tied for the lowest mean 10th-percentile omission rate (0.115 ± 0.091 SD). Its mean validation CBI was 0.093 ± 0.525 SD, with a training AUC of 0.862.

The LQHP configuration with a regularization multiplier of 0.5 achieved the same mean omission rate (0.115), with a slightly lower mean validation AUC (0.697) and CBI (0.046). The highest validation CBI (0.334) occurred with the LQHP configuration at a regularization multiplier of 1.0.

The lowest AICc (677.70) was achieved by the LQ configuration with a regularization multiplier of 0.5. This model had a mean validation AUC of 0.520 and CBI of −0.253, compared with 0.703 and 0.093, respectively, for the selected LQH model.
